review_text_raw:
What an intense game! When they said 'horror experience' they did not lie! Imagine yourself waking up one day and someone delivered a phone to you, and not any normal phone, it is a missing person's phone. The game starts off with you having Anna's phone, you played a video of her saying weird stuff and not to find her, however, when you go through her messages and dig deeper into her personal life, you will discover many things. Would you trust her boyfriend who seems to be worried or someone who she chatted with online? You will make this choice and end up with one of the four possible endings of this game. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997884297

The gameplay is all about texting, reading text messages, going to social media, solve some puzzles to find phone numbers, passwords or people to contact. It is a fun deep game and has lots of jumpscares! I gasped so many times and couldn't stop playing the game until I've finished it, and yes, that took me 9 hours to finish with little breaks in between. 

I was torn between the answers, yes you are limited with the answers they provided you but sometimes you wish to side with someone, the next moment you hear something from the other character which will make you suspect the first one. I ended up suspecting everyone including myself. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997329266

The actors were mediocre, none of them showed the supposed emotion the person would in such a situation, the facial expression wasn't the best especially Anna and Taylor. However the writing of the game and how the story flows is really good, I didn't expect that twist.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997329744

Pros:
+Well-written story.
+Jumpscares.
+Around 8 hours of gameplay.
+Multiple endings.
+High replay value. 
+Good puzzles.
+Steam achievements.

Cons:
-The characters are real people with mediocre acting.
-No hinting system.

I highly recommend this game, you can play it with your friend for a spooky weekend. I enjoyed it so much and still working on the rest of the achievements.

[b]Playing status:[/b] 100% achievement, 4x + playthroughs
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (16 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You found a lost phone. Inside, you find someone asking for help. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] puts you in the shoe of a stranger who is trying to find the owner of a lost phone. Will you succeed or will you fail?

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 4 endings with slight story branches
- New game plus let you play the game with faster chat speed

[b]Cons:[/b]
- No manual save and extra save slot to make it easier to unlock all endings
- Not suitable for people who have issues with flashing lights

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read a visual novel that was told through phone and chats, feel free to buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
As a game that is played out on a smartphone, the game does well to simulate the phone-like interface. It has a photo app, a contact book, a chat app - anything that you'll expect from a smartphone. Its functionality is limited tough. There is no option to switch between tabs nor a scroll bar on the right side of the screen to scroll the page faster.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is played out from series of chats. Expect a lot of typos and shortened words due to the informal context. This brings forth the characters' personality though, especially since everyone has a unique texting style from each other. Some information can also be retrieved by watching videos and receiving phone calls, although their voice is not expressive enough - it feels dragged out on purpose to make it easier for non-native English speakers to listen to. It does make them easier to hear, but it also kills their expression in the process.

Interface aside, the presentation helps with the storytelling. The glitchy screen and a few jumpscares help to set the mysterious vibe, while the surprising phone calls freak me out sometimes. It got toned down as you play the game, focusing more on the mysterious element. The writing was done well in regards to what's happening and sometimes, you will have several options to choose from. Despite giving the same outcome, the conversation will play out differently based on which option that you choose. However, some sentences are not flowing smoothly after choosing a certain option, giving you the impression that you chose the wrong one.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225479 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is focused on chatting with people and exploring everything that is inside the phone that you used. As I said before, sometimes you will have to choose between several options to proceed. Some of them will affect the endings, some are not. Some old chat and photos will also be encrypted, allowing you to play a minigame to restore their state, which takes form in arranging photos or word. It's quite easy to finish although some words might be difficult to arrange sometimes.

Hints are usually provided whenever you are stuck. You can ask people to figure out what you are supposed to do and they will gladly help you out. However, I got stuck twice with no idea to proceed. Although one is expected since I never do well with puzzles that have vague rules, another feels like they don't give enough hints to solve.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in ~4h, and proceed to replay the game several times to get all achievements. The new game+ helps a lot by providing a faster chat speed, allowing you to finish the game faster. However, you still need to wait for the voice-over near the ending to finish, and they talk very slowly. It was tiring to wait for them to finish talking and playing the game several times to unlock all four endings become not fun anymore. I wish there is an option to fast-forward the game at this point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225684 

[b]Problems[/b]
Although the game has a phone-like interface, some quality of life features are missing, notably the option to switch tabs in the browser (or the option to keep existing tab), and the feature to start a video from a certain timestamp. There were also some occasions when I had to type some forms and I couldn't use the tab button in my keyboard to switch between text boxes. Lastly, there are some flashing lights near the ending - people who have issues with it might want to stay out of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
For a visual novel game, it still can be enjoyed with people who don't like to read a wall of text. You might need to read a lot, but they are mostly in the form of short chats which shouldn't take long to finish. The story picks up an interesting topic that is enhanced with its mysterious vibe, and although the story feels weak at times, it still proves to be an enjoyable read.

review_text_raw:
[This review made after getting two bad endings out of 5 possible endings]

I like this game and I would recommend it, first and foremost, to players that are interested in STORY or, at least, world 
building. The game is not difficult: picture puzzles, word arranging, and some light fact searching comprise the bulk of the challenges. The meat of the game is in the dialogue choices, and this is where the replayability come from. You don't really get locked out of most options when taking/talking different ways, so you can express your moral flexibility without fearing that you'll reach a dead-end. As for content, they did a decent job of fleshing out with stuff that makes it feel like a "lived with" phone. The game does a good job of simulating smartphone usage with the apps, pics and their poses, vids, and social media content. A nice touch, is that there is a checklist of tasks that would help the truly clueless and serve as a guide for those looking for certain keystone events to play around with on subsequent playthroughs. This checklist is out of the way though for those who don't want hints on what to do next.


On the negative side, some of the voice acting, for me, was off if not "unsuitable". The delivery of the voice only lines truly felt and sounded "rehearsed". The VOs not sounding natural kind of sticks out like a sore thumb amid the aptness of the pictures and videos to a phone setting. The worst offender of this, sorry to say to the voice actor, is the Greg character. Truly, to me, it sounded like he was voicing a cartoon character instead of making a call, and it kind of took me out of the general mood of the game.

I think, the ending, will be pretty hit or miss for some people as well. I want to liken how the ending progresses to one of the scenes in a movie, but that would probably spoil it a bit. It's just that most people that saw it back then went "Wait what was that again?" Don't get me wrong, I'm fine with the endings I got (two bad endings), but the way to the climax was tedious, especially since I don't know if there is a message skip button for when you are doing a replay and you know what is going to be said. A note on the endings I got, it seems like you get locked to a set of outcomes after some threshold. I know my choices at the end didn't end up changing any of my final options. 

All in all, a decent casual horror sim game with some replayability, a fleshed out setting, hit or miss voice acting, and an endgame sequence (not ending, the stuff leading up to the ending) that'll make you go "excuse you? whowherewhenhowwhywhatnow?". 

For now, at full price, it would depend on your affinity for games like these to buy it for around a 5 hour single playthrough (worth it if you go with the $1 per hour of gameplay mindset). It is a decent recommend to buy if it ever has a sale at some point though.

Basically you find a phone, while you look into it you find out its from a woman called Anna who seems to be in trouble. Checking emails, decrypting messages, passwords and much more will unfold the story.

A short game but with replay value, and for the 3,50 currently on sale sure worth your time.

For the best experience you have to play this on your phone though.
It's also available on Android and IOS, their first game (Sara Is Missing) is even free on there!

review_text_raw:
Mostly liked this game.

There were a few good varied 'puzzles' for finding passwords etc, which I liked.

The storyline and dialogue was written so that i was never entirely sure who kidnapped the phone's owner.

On conclusion of the game, it was interesting to see what choices affected the outcome, and used that to try for alt. endings.
After the first completion, the game runs quicker on replay, tho wd have preferred ability to click thru the dialogues instead.
As there are no save points, there is no option but to replay the whole thing for alt. endings and achievements.
It was quicker the second time, due to knowing which files arent necessary to activate or find clues in.

Besides no skip scene options, the gameplay was intuitve and the production was good.
My only peeve was one of the characters. Tho he is supposed to be and ass, and i did get him to apologise to me, on the second run-thru (probably coz i had less patience for his bs) he rrreeealllly iritated me. Being an important character, there is no avoiding him and i just wanted to smack him in the head. So many times I wanted to just 'hang up' on him, tho there isnt that ability, and found myself actually talking back to him, in frustration of what a dick he is. Im all for 'everyone has their own individual paths and reasons for being who and where they are' as in 'you dont put down a baby for not knowing how to spell coz they're a baby' but he is such an ass - his type give men a bad name, ass.
So he is the reason for me mostly liking this game, and why im reluctant to replay for the remaining 9/23 achievements, as well as not being able to skip scenes, particularly towards the end.

If you like these 'Missing Phone Owner' games, and can tolerate a doosh, you will like this game.

Okay, so i just finished playing this (took me something like 5 or 6 hours I believe), and I felt compelled to review this game because it's like nothing I've played before. I had never heard of the "found-phone" genre in games before.

First let me say this: if you're a fan of mysteries, riddles, horror, or to be more specific, found-footage horror, then this game is for you! If not, try it anyway lol you just might be surprised.

This game starts out with you booting up a phone that was sent to you (or left on your doorstep, it's not totally cleared up in the story), and when you do it begins to glitch out a little and then these texts start coming in, and well, it just takes off from there...

The basic premise is that the owner of the phone, a girl named Anna, has gone missing and it's up to you (and a couple others along the way) to try to find her. You do this by digging through her phone and reading EVERYTHING, and then communicating with some of her contacts through texts and emails and an online dating app and a twitter-like app.  As things progress you learn that she has dissapeared and it may be connected to other recent dissapearances (but I won't go into more on that because I don't want to ruin the experience for new players).  Eventually, you realize there's a lot more going on than meets the eye.

The game has a very unnerving, intense feeling to it, and is all the better for it.  It has a decent story, some fun little mini games and riddles, a good amount of investigation and some pretty convinging dialogues, and for the REALLY hardcore sleuths out there, it even has some very interesting "easter eggs" hidden in the game that are quite rewarding to find. (I'll give you a hint here, but that's it...morse code, click it :)   )

As for graphics, sound, story, gameplay, etc...well graphics aren't important here as it's basically a phone emulator, the gameplay is as simple as digging through a phone and talking to people and looking stuff up (but you need a brain lol), the story is interesting enough that you really will never get bored in a single playthrough, and apparently it has many different endings so it has replayability there...where this game really shines though is the sound...it's incredible and really really well done.  When you start they recommend you use headphones, and I STRONGLY recommend you take their advice, it's just not the same on speakers, not even close

Anyway, the TL;DR is this:
if you 're looking for an action title, look elsewhere, but if you're looking for an EXPERIENCE that really makes you feel like you're a part of a mystery that needs to be solved, I can't recommend this highly enough. It's fun as hell!

For me it's a 4.5/5

A decent puzzle type game. While there are the occasional mild jump scares and something strange going on, it didn't really give me a horror or suspense vibe.

Pros:
- I generally stay away from FMV games, but the actresses & voice actors are actually pretty good
- The puzzle difficulty is OK for the most part
- Several other easter eggs and hidden puzzles if you want an extra challenge
- Has a mode for replaying to make text speed up instead of being at a realistic speed

Cons:
- Lacking in horror, and didn't feel that suspenseful
- Texts and responses when texting are often not quite right - grammatically wrong or just don't completely make sense. It could have used some more polish.
- Setting aside the fact that you're going through a stranger's phone instead of giving it to the police/family/etc, there are still things you have to do to progress the story that I would never think to do IRL
- While you frequently have different options for responses to messages, responses to what you say are frequently reused, giving the illusion of more choice than you really have. Good for role playing, but noticeable when replaying
- Has mutually exclusive achievements and different endings, but lacks replayability. Yes you can choose different dialogue option that can influence people differently, but the puzzles and their solutions are still the same.
- I wasn't a big fan of the ending. It didn't make much sense and wasn't really explained. That may have been saved for the second game though.

Verdict: 7/10

[h1]👍 Highly Recommended[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA is one of the few games that genuinely makes browsing through a smartphone feel fun. It's a horror game of sorts, but Instead of running from monsters or hiding in closets, you're piecing together the disappearance of a young woman by exploring every corner of her phone. Messages, photos, videos, emails, social media, and browser history slowly reveal a mystery that's equal parts psychological thriller and supernatural horror. It feels disturbingly believable-almost like scrolling through someone else's real device.[/i]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🟢 PROS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Brilliant Found Phone Concept:[/b] Investigating an entire mystery through a lost smartphone is an incredibly immersive idea that still feels unique years after release.
[*][b]Excellent Storytelling:[/b] The narrative unfolds naturally through text messages, emails, videos, and social media instead of lengthy exposition. Every app contains another piece of the puzzle.
[*][b]Convincing Characters:[/b] Conversations feel surprisingly authentic. Friends, coworkers, and family all have believable personalities and motivations, making the investigation feel personal.
[*][b]Genuinely Creepy:[/b] SIMULACRA builds tension through unsettling discoveries, disturbing videos, and the feeling that something is deeply wrong with the phone itself.
[*][b]Creative Puzzles:[/b] Unlocking files, recovering deleted data, solving passwords, and navigating fake apps keeps the gameplay engaging throughout.
[*][b]Multiple Endings:[/b] Your decisions matter, giving the story additional replay value.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🔴 CONS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Live-Action Acting Can Be Uneven:[/b] Most performances are convincing, but a handful of scenes feel slightly awkward compared to the otherwise strong production.
[*][b]Occasional Interface Frustrations:[/b] Searching through apps or revisiting conversations can sometimes be more cumbersome than necessary.
[*][b]The Ending May Divide Players:[/b] Without spoilers, the final revelations won't satisfy everyone, especially those hoping for a more grounded explanation.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]💰 VALUE FOR MONEY[/h2]
[b]Excellent[/b] — SIMULACRA offers several hours of engaging investigation packed with memorable moments, clever puzzles, and one of the most original horror concepts in the genre. It's frequently discounted on Steam, making it an even easier recommendation for fans of narrative adventures and psychological horror.
[hr][/hr]
[h3]⭐ 9/10[/h3]
[i]A brilliantly executed smartphone horror that proves the scariest place in a horror game isn't an abandoned mansion. Immersive, unsettling, and remarkably original, SIMULACRA remains one of the most engaging narrative horror experiences available on Steam.[/i]

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. I am generally biased to be forgiving of FMV interactive movies, so of course I've played others like Her Story, #WarGames, The Bunker, Late Shift, and The Shapeshifting Detective.  Like those games, this game is relatively short on total content, with moments of good acting and then...well, near-miss moments that make you cringe.  Also, these games tend to have multiple achievements and scenes that you can't get in one playthrough, which is a way of extending the replay value, but I seldom feel particularly inclined to watch the repeated parts over and over again.

This game is unique due to the phone interface and the clever design that it took to make that work.  You feel like it really could be you deciding what to do in this situation, but then sometimes you're reminded how you can't actually do anything like answer a phone call.  So when it works, it's great, but it has built-in limitations to just how far the concept can go.  I commend them for the creepy story.  I wish the really uneven voice acting hadn't pulled me out of it from time to time.  At least Anna (whose phone you've found) is done consistently well.

Your first full playthrough will take 3-4 hours depending on how much you read, and subsequent plays should take you a bit less.  Alternate achievements, videos, conversations, and endings are basically earned by the responses you choose, like who to be nice to, who to scold, and who to trust.  The downside of that is like the decisions in Telltale games, especially The Walking Dead: you'll have to replay with lots of choices that you'd never make in real life if you want to see the other paths.  In that regard, replays are more like gaming the game and less like experiencing the story.  But overall, that's a complaint that's bound to be true of every choose-your-own-adventure game you can find.  So you know what you're getting.  If you like that, and you have a tolerance for FMV games, this one is certainly worth $5.

review_text_raw:
A decent puzzle type game. While there are the occasional mild jump scares and something strange going on, it didn't really give me a horror or suspense vibe.

Pros:
- I generally stay away from FMV games, but the actresses & voice actors are actually pretty good
- The puzzle difficulty is OK for the most part
- Several other easter eggs and hidden puzzles if you want an extra challenge
- Has a mode for replaying to make text speed up instead of being at a realistic speed

Cons:
- Lacking in horror, and didn't feel that suspenseful
- Texts and responses when texting are often not quite right - grammatically wrong or just don't completely make sense. It could have used some more polish.
- Setting aside the fact that you're going through a stranger's phone instead of giving it to the police/family/etc, there are still things you have to do to progress the story that I would never think to do IRL
- While you frequently have different options for responses to messages, responses to what you say are frequently reused, giving the illusion of more choice than you really have. Good for role playing, but noticeable when replaying
- Has mutually exclusive achievements and different endings, but lacks replayability. Yes you can choose different dialogue option that can influence people differently, but the puzzles and their solutions are still the same.
- I wasn't a big fan of the ending. It didn't make much sense and wasn't really explained. That may have been saved for the second game though.

Verdict: 7/10

Little FMV interactive story telling game from Asian Devs, where you have to play like a Stalker / Hacker who finds a stranger's phone and has to find out what happened to the original owner.
Probably brings about 2-3 hours of semi-original fun for the main story line and one ending (of four), well worth it for the cheap price (if it's on sale) - I for instance bought Simulacra 1+2 for only 1.2€ and am already happy getting my money's worth after playing only the first part, gonna play the second one too, but beware the most expensive and newest third part is supposedly crappy according to reviews, so not gonna bother with that one.

+ neat little game, cheap price, semi-original story and idea

+ multiple Endings, somewhat of replayability (though not much)

+ some interesting charachters, an unknown protagonist, possible similarities to real live 
   dating crimes (educational)

+ some interesting Achievements in and outside of the main story line

+ nice positive review link @ the end if you liked the game & none if you click on didn't like it^^

+ very good price (at least while on sale or from external site) for Part 1&2 (not 3 though)

  or starting a vlog video while simultaneously getting a call freezes screen sideways so it gets 
  stuck and you have to restart from last checkpoint

  mostly you get like 3 Dialog options for chats etc., but in most cases it will all result in the same, maybe one 
  added sentence or a word or two changed and stuff like that


All in all I do recommend it to anyone who likes FMV / interactive and/or invesitgative / mystery Genre games.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Short but Intuitive Mystery Game[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA[/i] is a modern FMV game that features great sleuthing gameplay with some minor horror elements. After I 100% the entire game, I can safely say this is one of the better indie visual novel titles I've encountered if not for the gameplay alone. I will try to keep this review mostly spoiler-free, but as usual with my reviews for narrative-based games, I will have spoilers for stuff I feel the need to comment on. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The gameplay and puzzles are fun yet intuitive. I like the process of fixing corrupted messages and images to not only progress the game but to also discover more about the characters.
[*] Lots of "show don't tell" moments that exemplify how the developers understand that this is a visual medium and that it is important to use the visuals to their advantage. For example, though it's never stated Anna is into fitness, one of the first image puzzles is of her posing with weights to give the idea that she is an active person. This is great  yet subtle storytelling I love to see in these types of games. 
[*] The text messages and dating profiles are pretty genuine. There are definitely people out there who act exactly like the ones in this game.
[*] The narrative does a lot to try and make you question the motives of the characters and their backgrounds in a meaningful way so that the suspense is maintained the entire playthrough. 
[*] [spoiler] The main antagonist being a serial killer HAL-9000-esque AI in the phone itself is fascinating in its own right, and the fact that its goal is to create perfect versions of otherwise "pathetic worms" as it refers to people it deems as as such, is great social commentary on how people are obsessed with their public image online to the point that they are no longer genuinely themselves. The antagonist also serves as a personification of tech companies and their obsession to mold people into their idealized image through deceptive practices and establishing trust by packaging things in digestible ways. For example, during the phone reset, the soothing sounds and use of cool hues is meant to contrast with the otherwise invasive questions and disturbing content the OS system tries to get you to answer in detail. In the end, you get the best ending by impressing the AI with your ability to manipulate the characters--an interesting moral dilemma to say the least!  [/spoiler]
[*] The menus and apps look and feel like their real version counterparts. Very good overall graphical presentation. 
[*] Small and subtle changes to show you are progressing through the story. For example, [spoiler] Anna's picture in the home screen will change expression the closer you get to the ending of the game. [/spoiler]
[*] Lots of small things to discover just by exploring the phone (which you can get achievements for). 
[*] Sped up dialog loading for additional playthroughs is a great QoL feature. 
[/olist]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The voice acting and FMV sequences come across as cheesy most of the time, if not overacted. 
[*] The autosave feature means you can't go back to a previous part like you can with most visual novels. This means that if you messed up on a certain decision, you may have to restart the entire run just to redo it. This can be pretty frustrating. 
[*] No option to skip puzzles for additional playthroughs means you'll have to do them over and over again which can be pretty tedious if you're trying to get all the achievements. 
[*] The dialogue choices you  need to appease and have Taylor trust you come across as a bit too flirty at times.
[*] Greg and Ashley come across as too angry and distrustful to the player character depending on certain choices made. Meanwhile, Taylor comes across as too trusting. This is why sometimes it's not very good to have a faceless protagonist--we don't really understand what the characters see in [i]you[/i] when the interactions are so minimal. 
[*] The horror elements are too on the nose with the jumpscares. Though the phone OS does have some good subtle horror elements, more of this throughout the game would have been way better overall. 
[*] [spoiler] Though I like the idea of the antagonist, having it type in predictable shaky font and using distorted visuals is pretty cliche. Personally, I think it'd come across scarier if it were way more subtle like how it is when the phone resets.[/spoiler]
[/olist]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Worth at least one playthrough--though playing it blind is your best bet. The gameplay alone makes it worth it. For additional playthroughs, some patience is required. Watch additional endings via recordings if that's not your thing.

Having played "A Normal Lost Phone", the concept of Simulacra isn't anything new to me, however due to this not being a particularly common way of making a game it is a welcome addition to this genre of sorts. 
Simulacra also comes with a couple of different twists compared to what "A Normal Lost Phone" had so it's not complete copy.

The good:
*You are thrown into an interesting story that you have to go through with the help of strangers. Who should you trust? Who should you be weary of? Wel that's the beauty, you don't know and you have to base your judgements on scraps of information that you can find. The story is definitely one of the highlights of this game.
*The gameplay whilst isn't groundbreaking works well for this game and doesn't propose any friction for the player on how to proceed.
*There's a decent bit of replayability in this game if you want to uncover all of the different paths. They also aren't particularly difficult to reach if given enough thought.

The bad:
*The horror elements of this game... Don't get me wrong, I love myself some horror and this game seems like a good candidate for a bit of it, however the way it is implemented in this specific game is forced and cliche.
Build tension through uneasiness, not through awful jumpscares.
*I don't need to be redirected to a webpage with a Discord server every time I finish the game. It is annoying. If I want to join your Discord Ill find a way to do it without it being showed in my face every time.
*For a game with so many branching I feel like it should've had a save system. If you want to get a specific achievement you are forced to replay the whole game. It is remedied by the faster conversations, but I do not want to listen to the same conversation for 7 times just so I can get an achievement.
*The acting leaves some things to be desired. I understand that this is an indie game but the video segments in this game felt somewhat robotic and lifeless.

Overall, Simulacra is a fun and interesting little game, that will not burn a hole in your wallet and will keep you entertained for a day or two. I think its worth giving a try, if you can stand the occasional jumpscare.

review_text_raw:
[i]Simulacra[/i] is a captivating puzzle-slash-detective-slash-horror-slash-social commentary game which is yours to enjoy for a delightfully economic entree fee.

So you found a phone on your doorstep and it appears to belong to the now missing twenty-something Anna. Your quest to find out what happened to her will take place entirely through the smartphone interface, trying to get into contact with her familiars, sifting through her social media posts and recovering lost files. Soon enough the mysteries start to pile up. Those who have a basic grasp of the philosophy of Jean Baudrillard may already guess what's behind the sudden disappearance.

It's a short game which will take approximately 4-5 hours to finish, which is enough to get involved with the characters while still short enough so that the gameplay does not grow stale. There is replay value to be had, since your decisions (who to trust, what to do) can take the story to different conclusions.

The game touches on a few social issues, such as [spoiler]sexual harassment[/spoiler], [spoiler]the banality of social media content[/spoiler] and [spoiler]the ongoing digitization of society[/spoiler], but I never found the game to be either too preachy or too political. There is also some existential philosophy woven into the dialogues, though it's enough to give you something to muse about, it's too little to be considered profound. The puzzles are fairly easy, making the game more appealing to casual gamers rather than seasoned point-and-click fanatics.

At the bottom of all its qualities are certainly the jump scares. While it can be argued that this much loathed trope does the trick (i.e.: keeping you on edge even during the quiet moments), they are still a cheap substitute for the subtleties of psychological horror. That said, the game did manage to frighten me through the sheer eeriness of a digital device continually distorting into absolute madness, but the rather bland acting in the audio/video files often pulled me out of suspense-belief and back into the comfort zone.

[b][u]Final verdict:[/u] 7/10[/b]. [i]Simulacra[/i] is a fresh and well-executed, though somewhat poorly acted missing person mystery.

Honestly a fun little horror game that's worth the price of admission. I'm a sucker for games like this involving fake OS' and learning its quirks and involving myself in this pseudo world of fake apps and this game pulls it off quite well. 

My original run in with this game was watching a twitch streamer named MOONMOON play through it on Halloween back when it first came out and I remember enjoying watching him play through it. So much so that I would rewatch the stream while it was still available in the archives. 

My only gripes with the game are minor and honestly just wanting more things to do. I wanted to explore more of the apps and more websites inside this universe, but kept getting cut off and I would just be like aww okay. I loved the idea of the pseudo Twitter named "Jabbr" and how you can just openly respond to people. What I would've loved more is if the people actually responded to you in some form or fashion, even if its just some default responses, its better than just no one ever saying anything. 

My only other negative I would say is [spoiler] the villain or the Simulacra as you can call it is honestly a bit goofy. The idea of him is interesting but his ramblings and ideology as he just sits there and spews it to you sounds like someone who thinks their better than everyone ramble on about what perfect utopia they want. It just comes off as whiny and a bit silly. Also, during repeat runs, its a bit annoying that I can't skip its dialogue at all. It gets annoying listening to him say the same things over and over and I wish I could fast text through it like you can with the text messages themselves in NG+ [/spoiler]

Took me a while to finally sit and play it myself and I'm glad I did. Even though I knew what was going to happen, I still thoroughly enjoyed my time with it and I'm very excited to see what the sequel adds to it.

Unsettling. Unseen horrors. You feel as though you truly found someone's phone and have to uncover all their dark secrets to find out what happened. 

Simulacra is an amazing little rabbit hole of a game; a found‑phone thriller that feels intimate, invasive, and surprisingly reactive. Even though my first playthrough ended in the bad ending, with both Taylor and Anna dying, it didn’t sour the experience at all. If anything, it made me realize just how many branching paths and character‑shaping choices I’d only brushed past.

What stands out most is how much influence you actually have over the people you’re texting. The tone you take, the pressure you apply, the empathy you show (or don’t); it all ripples outward in ways that feel organic rather than scripted. That makes every conversation feel like a little puzzle of its own, and it’s easy to get pulled into the illusion that you’re really trying to save someone on the other end of the screen.

There’s also a surprising amount of content tucked into the phone that I completely missed on my first run. I was so worried about the battery dying that I missed returning to the emails and missed the final vlog. That tension is part of the charm, though;  the sense that you’re racing against something truly evil on the other side of the screen.

The result is a game with genuine replayability. Multiple endings, branching character arcs, and hidden threads make it worth diving back in, especially once you know the stakes and can explore the phone more confidently.
If you like narrative mysteries with a voyeuristic twist and choices that actually matter, Simulacra is absolutely worth your time;  even if your first ending is a tragic one.

review_text_raw:
This was certainly a unique idea for the game: figuring out what happened to the owner of the phone you picked up by going through the history of her chats and speaking to people on her contact list. The puzzles are intuitive and the game doesn't hold your hand in solving them, so its very satisfying when you get that "EUREKA!" moment as you remember a detail mentioned off-handledy in one of the documents you read hours later.

Yes, the gameplay is thrilling, but I wish it was attached to a more interesting plot. Anna's personal life amounts to standard relationship problems, which wouldn't be such a problem if the characters were more interesting. A troubled girl... her cheating boyfreiend... her supportive friends... and a jokester. All standard horror-movie players and despite games attempts to give them some depth, they just weren't all that engaging. 

There's also the obligatory twist ending. The game does good job building up the mystery and tension of what happened to Anna... but the resolution is rather silly. In general for a horror game its not particularly scary as it mostly relies on predictable jump scares.

Despite the basic premise, the game is quite lengthy (my first playthrough was over 4 houts long) and there's a a bit of replay value to it as some puzzles have several ways to solve depending on what plot choices you make.

7/10 (Mostly for the gameplay and presentation)

The first playthrough is the most fun because you get to explore the game's limits and be a catfishing detective, although the replay value is pretty low for me because then you realize just how short it really is. For $5 though, it is acceptable. The buildup is great and the ending is decent and not what I expected, but pretty original in its own way. I also think they did a great job with the interface and laid out relatively natural methods for you to do your investigating. The journey was definitely better than the destination for me.

I am a fan of interactive storytelling, but the only thing you really feel invested in is finding out what happened to Anna, and if you're sympathetic, wanting to save her, since she is the only character you really get to know through all your interactions and discoveries. The biggest con for me is that the acting and voice acting was okay at best - at times a little too animated/forced - and I felt if there were more development for the characters, the attachment would truly tear us apart as we are forced to make more choices. Also, the creep factor disappeared for me personally once I got through to the ending.

Overall, I do recommend the game, but not very enthusiastically. It was good, but has a lot of potential to be even better.

This is more of a meh than a thumb up, but this will have to do.

The story is decent, the game is more or less well executed. There are several annoyances and bugs that can piss you off severely, but nothing game breaking. Although it sports 4-5 endings, there's not much in terms of replayability, and the only replayability you'll find is you going back trying to unlock different stuff, although very little changes in terms of narrative.

On the technical side, the PC port kind of sucks in several aspects: tabbing doesn't move you through different textboxes, backspacing erases entire words, the sound is MIND NUMBINGLY HIGH and there is no volume slider anywhere to be found (I literally played at 1/100 volume with my headphones, and it almost did my head in), occasional bugs with event music not stopping (yay, the screeches and white noises!) or completely freezing (yay, the kill & restarts!).

With that being said the first playthrough is quite enjoyable, and the game is rather cheap, so I couldn't not recommend it. Although I'd still bash the damned phone screen on every voice dialogue or unskippable video (me having to trial and error 7-8 entire playthroughs didn't help, probably). Hopefully it will get fixed in the future or in eventual future iterations of the game.

review_text_raw:
I absolutely love both games that come with uncovering lore and mystery as well as characters you can really deeply care for, even if you're mostly contacting them through text.
Simulacra is definitely a story game over a gameplay game -- most of the controls are point and click and most of the "game type" puzzles are rather simple. Simulacra really shines through in its story -- uncovering the overarching mystery behind the disappearance of the phone's original owner, Anna. The game also has replayability with four different endings (Though I've only seen two of them thus far), that change with your actions throughout the game.

Probably my only complaint would be that some of the calls and voice messages can have a bit of hokey acting in them, which can draw you out of the game a bit (Except for Taylor, his actor is pretty awesome).

Overall I'd definitely say it's well worth the price if you're looking for an interesting modern mystery to settle down with, as well as a few spooks now and then.

review_text_raw:

This is a strait forward puzzle game where one has to dig through a stranger’s phone, and talk to third parties through their device, to unlock the mystery of their disappearance. Over all this isn’t a hard game to figure out and a single play through can be competed in a couple hours with minimal effort. 

Additional play throughs are sped up with a “Begin +” mode; Which makes messages appear faster but there are a ton of unskippable moments that make achievement hunting a chore. That second, and third, play through was rough… 

Worth  a couple bucks for a single play through, but, regardless of ending, it’s painful to get through multiple times. If there was a way to skip the redundancy, this would have been a perfect achievement hunters’ game.

- Enjoyable
- Intriguing

The puzzles are creative enough, and the story is well-written and suspenseful – except for the finale when they decide to explain everything and then it goes downhill. The weakest content are the video segments; Anna is fine most of the time but the Taylor guy is a bad actor and some other voiceovers are pretty weak too.

Despite having multiple endings, the game has almost no replayability. The game is strictly linear and although you can speed up the text on your second playthrough, it's still tedious as hell to click through all those identical texts and puzzles just to see another ending. Play through the game once and then forget about it.
